title: How to Test an Evolutionary Explanation

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: {{c1::Natural selection}} is a consistent difference in survival or reproduction among individuals that differ in a trait.
cards.quote: Natural selection is a consistent difference in survival or reproduction among individuals that differ in a trait.

cards.front: The currency of natural selection is {{c1::fitness}}: reproductive success, the number of surviving offspring an individual leaves in a given environment.
cards.quote: Its currency is fitness: reproductive success, the number of surviving offspring an individual leaves in a given environment.

cards.front: In the 1977 Daphne Major drought, larger medium ground finches with larger beaks survived best. Why can that survival comparison not say whether beak size was the target of selection?
cards.back: Beak size and body size go together, so survival shows selection on the measured traits or on traits correlated with them, without saying which.
cards.quote: beak size and body size go together, so survival alone cannot say which was the target.

cards.front: How is the selection differential S that predicts the offspring defined?
cards.back: The mean of the parents, each counted once for every offspring it contributed, minus the mean of the population before selection.
cards.quote: the mean of the parents, each counted once for every offspring it contributed, minus the mean of the population before selection

cards.front: When does the difference between the survivors' mean and the pre-selection mean equal the selection differential S?
cards.back: Only if the survivors contribute about equally to the next generation, because S counts each parent once for every offspring it leaves.
cards.quote: The survivor difference equals S only if the survivors contribute about equally, as the worked examples below assume.

cards.front: After a drought, large-beaked survivors leave more offspring each than small-beaked survivors. How does S compare with the simple survivor-minus-population difference, and why?
cards.back: S is larger. S counts each parent once per offspring, so the prolific large-beaked parents pull the parental mean up; the survivor comparison measures only the survival part of selection.
cards.quote: That comparison measures only the survival part of selection.

cards.front: In a parent-offspring regression for beak depth, what is the mid-parent value?
cards.back: The average of a chick's two parents' trait values, plotted against the chick's own adult beak depth.
cards.quote: Plot each chick's adult beak depth against the average of its two parents, the mid-parent value.

cards.front: What does the slope of offspring beak depth on mid-parent beak depth estimate, and on what condition?
cards.back: Narrow-sense heritability (h²), but only if parents and chicks do not share an environment that also shapes the trait.
cards.why: The slope is how many millimetres the chick's beak rises for each millimetre the parents' average rises.
cards.quote: estimates the film's dial, narrow-sense heritability (h²), but only if parents and chicks do not share an environment that also shapes the trait

cards.front: Why can survival data alone never show that a trait is inherited?
cards.back: Inheritance needs a comparison among relatives, such as parents and their offspring, and survival data contain no such comparison.
cards.quote: This needs a comparison among relatives, which survival data lack.

cards.front: Keller and colleagues found that {{c1::twenty percent}} of the offspring in their Daphne Major sample were extra-pair young, whose social father was not the genetic father.
cards.back: Found by typing birds at eight microsatellite loci.
cards.quote: Twenty percent of the offspring in their sample were extra-pair young, whose social father was not the genetic father.

cards.front: In the Daphne Major finch study by Keller and colleagues, which way did wrongly assigned fathers bias heritability estimates, and why?
cards.back: Downward: the traits looked less inherited than they are, because chicks were being compared with males who were not their genetic fathers.
cards.quote: In this study, wrong fathers made the traits look less inherited than they are (figure).

cards.front: What is a maternal effect? Give two examples from finches.
cards.back: An influence of the mother on her offspring other than her genes, such as egg size or the food she brings.
cards.quote: maternal effects, influences of the mother other than her genes, such as egg size or the food she brings

cards.front: Large-beaked mother finches bring their chicks more food, and food also deepens beaks. Heritability is estimated from mother-offspring resemblance. What happens to the estimate, and why?
cards.back: It is too high. A maternal effect that tracks the mother's own trait adds resemblance that is not genetic, so the trait looks more inherited than it is.
cards.quote: A maternal effect that tracks the mother's own trait can make a trait look more inherited than it is.

cards.front: What are microsatellite loci, and why were they useful in the Daphne Major finch pedigree?
cards.back: Places in the genome where short repeated stretches of DNA vary between individuals. Typing them assigns each chick its genetic father.
cards.quote: places in the genome where short repeated stretches of DNA vary between individuals

cards.front: The breeder's equation, {{c1::R = h² × S}}, predicts how far the next generation's mean moves.
cards.back: R is the response, h² narrow-sense heritability, S the selection differential.
cards.quote: The breeder's equation, R = h² × S, predicts how far the next generation's mean moves

cards.front: Why does a nonrandom difference in survival show selection but not yet evolution?
cards.back: For a trait's average to evolve, the trait must be inherited and the offspring generation measured; survival shows only that selection happened.
cards.quote: A nonrandom difference in survival shows selection, not yet evolution.

cards.front: To show that selection changed a trait's average, which three claims are needed, and which quantity of the breeder's equation goes with each?
cards.back: Selection happened (S), the trait is inherited (h²), and the offspring changed (R). Each needs its own evidence.
cards.quote: selection happened (S), the trait is inherited (h²), and the offspring changed (R)

cards.front: Illustrative finch population: mean beak depth before a drought is 9.40 mm. The survivors that breed, contributing about equally, average 9.80 mm, and h² is 0.60. Predict the offspring mean.
cards.quote: Before a drought, adult mean beak depth in a finch population is 9.40 mm.

cards.front: Illustrative bird population: mean beak depth is 12.0 mm. Survivors that breed, contributing about equally, average 11.5 mm, and h² is 0.50. Predict the offspring mean.
cards.why: R has the same sign as S, so selection for smaller beaks predicts a smaller offspring mean.
cards.quote: a population averages 9.40 mm and the drought survivors that breed 9.20 mm

cards.front: Illustrative population: mean bill depth 15.0 mm before selection; breeding survivors, contributing about equally, average 16.0 mm; their offspring, raised in similar conditions, average 15.3 mm. What heritability does this response imply?
cards.quote: a fraction h² of the selection differential S

cards.front: Pre-drought mean 9.40 mm, breeding survivors 9.80 mm. A student predicts an offspring mean of 10.00 mm. What is wrong?
cards.back: The offspring mean lies beyond the survivors' mean, so R (0.60 mm) exceeds S (0.40 mm): the student implicitly used h² = 0.60 / 0.40 = 1.5, above 1.
cards.why: R must lie between 0 and S.
cards.quote: If your offspring mean lies beyond the survivors' mean, you have used a heritability above 1.

cards.front: Within what scope does the single-trait breeder's equation R = h² × S apply?
cards.back: One trait, one population, one episode of directional selection; an additive model; offspring raised in the same environment as their parents; no unmeasured correlated trait that also affects fitness.
cards.quote: an additive model, in which the effects of genes simply add up; offspring raised in the same environment as their parents

cards.front: Offspring of drought-selected finches grow up in a year of abundant food and turn out larger than predicted by R = h² × S. Does this refute the prediction?
cards.back: No. The test is outside the equation's scope: only an offspring sample raised in an unchanged environment tests the prediction, and better food could enlarge the offspring by itself.
cards.quote: Only an actual offspring sample, raised in an unchanged environment, tests the prediction.

cards.front: In 2006 the Grants reported that medium ground finches diverged in beak size from the large ground finch 22 years after it arrived on Daphne Major. How did the observed change compare with the breeder's equation?
cards.back: The response came close to the value predicted from beak-size heritability, so the equation predicted well over a single episode of selection.
cards.why: The two species had severely depleted their shared food.
cards.quote: the response came close to the value predicted from beak-size heritability

cards.front: Drought favoured large beaks in medium ground finches in 1977, but small pointed beaks survived best in the 1985 drought. Why did selection reverse?
cards.back: The wet El Niño of 1982 and 1983 left a seed supply dominated by small soft seeds. As far as the record shows, the remaining seeds, not drought itself, set the direction.
cards.quote: Drought did not favour large beaks as such; as far as the record shows, the seeds that remained did.
cards.section: The direction of selection can reverse

cards.front: Why does R = h² × S predict one generation of finch beak evolution but not a decade?
cards.back: The environment sets S afresh each time, and unpredictable fluctuations (rains, hybridization, a competitor's arrival) set its sign and size.
cards.quote: R = h² × S carries a population one generation forward from an S that the environment sets afresh each time.
cards.section: The direction of selection can reverse

cards.front: In a drought like 1985, breeding survivors have smaller beaks than the pre-drought mean, and beak depth is highly heritable. Which way does the offspring mean move, and how far at most?
cards.back: Toward smaller beaks. S is negative, so R is negative too, and R lies between 0 and S: the offspring mean falls but no further than the survivors' mean.
cards.why: Rests on R = h² × S with 0 ≤ h² ≤ 1.
cards.quote: R must lie between 0 and S. It is 0 only if h² is 0; otherwise it has the same sign as S.

cards.front: In finches, beak depth and body size are correlated. Suppose selection acts only on body size, but you apply the single-trait breeder's equation to beak depth. What do you see?
cards.back: An apparent response in beak depth that is really a by-product of selection on body size, so the single-trait prediction is unreliable.
cards.quote: so selection on body size could show up as an apparent response in beak depth
cards.section: The direction of selection can reverse

cards.front: Why can the Daphne Major finch record not say for certain what did the selecting, and how could such a question be settled?
cards.back: The remaining seeds are the leading suspect, but 1977 cannot be rerun. Where a proposed cause can be moved, an experiment can test it.
cards.quote: The finch record cannot say for certain what did the selecting: the remaining seeds are the leading suspect, and 1977 cannot be rerun.
cards.section: The direction of selection can reverse

cards.front: Name the three kinds of evidence used to test evolutionary explanations.
cards.back: Observation of natural variation, experimental contrast, and historical inference.
cards.quote: The second film set observation of natural variation, experimental contrast and historical inference side by side.
cards.section: Three kinds of evidence, and what each can carry

cards.front: Guppies are moved into a stream reach with a different predator regime and compared with their source population years later. Which kind of evidence is this, and what makes it so?
cards.back: Experimental contrast. The proposed cause, the predator regime, was deliberately changed, rather than compared across sites that differ naturally.
cards.quote: Where a proposed cause can be moved, an experiment can test it.
cards.section: The direction of selection can reverse

cards.front: What did the guppy transplant not show, and what did later work by Reznick's group find about it?
cards.back: How the predators acted. Guppies at sites with predators of adults die at higher rates at every size, and the resulting change in population density helps explain the evolution.
cards.quote: guppies at sites with predators of adults die at higher rates at every size, not mainly as adults
cards.section: Three kinds of evidence, and what each can carry

cards.front: When can historical inference discriminate between rival evolutionary explanations?
cards.back: Only when there are traces that the rival explanations predict differently.
cards.why: Carol Cleland argued this is a different method from experiment, not a weaker one.
cards.quote: Historical inference works only with traces that rival explanations predict differently.
cards.section: Three kinds of evidence, and what each can carry

cards.front: A male finch arrived on Daphne Major and bred with a resident medium ground finch. Which part of this story was observed and which was inferred, and from what?
cards.back: The breeding was watched. His origin was inferred: his genome placed him as a Geospiza conirostris from Española, more than 100 km away.
cards.quote: The breeding was watched. His origin was inferred.
cards.section: Three kinds of evidence, and what each can carry

cards.front: Fish from a transplanted stream population mature later and larger than wild fish from the source reach. Design a result that would show the difference is inherited, and name the principle.
cards.back: Rear descendants of both populations in a common lab setting; a difference that persists in a common environment is the best evidence it is inherited. Inheritance can be read only when relatives do not share an environment that shapes the trait.
cards.quote: but only if parents and chicks do not share an environment that also shapes the trait

cards.front: What can a DNA-checked parent-offspring regression on Daphne Major finches not show?
cards.back: What did the selecting. It can also still mistake a shared environment for inheritance, because parents rear their own chicks.
cards.quote: It cannot identify what did the selecting, and it can still mistake a shared environment for inheritance, because parents rear their own chicks.

cards.front: A genome study of Daphne Major finches found six large-effect loci explaining 45 percent of beak-size variation in the medium ground finch. What does this leave unexplained?
cards.back: Most of the variation is unassigned, and an association with a locus is not a mechanism.
cards.quote: That leaves most of the variation unassigned, and an association with a locus is not a mechanism.

cards.front: From the 30-year Daphne Major record, a writer concludes that selection on Darwin's finches oscillates everywhere. What does the record actually support?
cards.back: Only that selection varied in direction and pattern on one island, in two species, over those years. Other islands and lineages are outside the data.
cards.quote: that selection varied in direction and pattern on one island, in two species, over those years

cards.front: A hybrid finch lineage on Daphne Major bred only among itself within three generations. A student calls it a new species and says speciation takes three generations. What does the evidence support?
cards.back: Reproductive isolation in this case only. Not that the lineage will persist or is a new species, nor any general timescale for speciation.
cards.quote: but not that the lineage will persist or is a new species, nor any general timescale for speciation

cards.front: For a survival count, a heritability estimate and a forecast of next year's selection, where does the main uncertainty sit in each?
cards.back: Survival count: sample size. Heritability: pedigree errors and shared environments. Forecast: next year's weather.
cards.quote: sample size in a survival count, pedigree errors and shared environments in a heritability, the next year's weather in a forecast

cards.front: Finch eggs are swapped between deep-beaked and shallow-beaked nests, and chicks are measured as adults. What slopes on genetic and foster parents do the genes-only, rearing-only and both hypotheses predict?
cards.back: Genes only: genetic-parent slope positive, foster slope near zero. Rearing only: the reverse. Both: both slopes positive, and comparing them shows roughly how much each matters.
cards.why: Cross-fostering separates genes from rearing; fathers must be assigned by DNA.
cards.quote: If genes alone explain the resemblance, the slope on genetic parents is positive and the slope on foster parents near zero.

cards.front: A cross-fostering study swaps finch eggs soon after laying. Which non-genetic sources of parent-offspring resemblance can it still not remove?
cards.back: Effects of the mother through the egg, since swapping happens after laying; differences in territory and food between foster nests. The estimate also belongs to one island, species, cohort and environment.
cards.quote: swapping happens after the egg is laid, so effects of the mother through the egg remain

cards.front: Illustrative finches: females' selection differential is 0.2 mm and males' is 0.6 mm (each parent leaving equal offspring), h² = 0.50, with no sex-specific inheritance. Predict R, and the error from using the males' S alone.
cards.back: S = (0.2 + 0.6) / 2 = 0.4 mm; R = 0.50 × 0.4 = 0.2 mm. Using 0.6 mm gives 0.3 mm, an overprediction.
cards.why: The offspring S is the average of the two sexes' differentials.
cards.quote: Using only the larger differential, when both point the same way, overpredicts the response.
cards.section: When the sexes are selected differently

cards.front: Why did Morrissey and colleagues favour the Robertson-Price identity over the multivariate breeder's equation?
cards.back: The multivariate equation is valid only if every correlated trait affecting fitness is measured. The identity predicts the response from the genetic covariance between the trait and fitness itself.
cards.quote: it predicts the response from the genetic covariance between the trait and fitness itself

cards.front: Offspring of 1977 drought survivors, raised after a wet year with plentiful seeds, are larger than the pre-drought mean. Name two reasons this alone does not prove that selection on beak size changed the population.
cards.back: The offspring grew up in a different environment, so food could explain the change; and an unmeasured correlated trait such as body size may have been the real target.
cards.why: Both break the breeder's equation's scope conditions.
cards.quote: offspring raised in the same environment as their parents; and no unmeasured trait, correlated with this one, that also affects fitness
